entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10411"/><div sID="gen18572" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10411"/><hi type="bold">3. Zedekiah ... sent--</hi>fearing lest, in the event of the Chaldeans overcoming Pharaoh-hophra, they should return to besiege Jerusalem. See on <reference osisRef="Jer.21.1">Jr 21:1</reference>; that chapter chronologically comes in between the thirty-seventh and thirty-eighth chapter. The message of the king to Jeremiah here in the thirty-seventh chapter is, however, somewhat earlier than that in the twenty-first chapter; here it is while the issue between the Chaldeans and Pharaoh was undecided; there it is when, after the repulse of Pharaoh, the Chaldeans were again advancing against Jerusalem; hence, while Zephaniah is named in both embassies, Jehucal accompanies him here, Pashur there. But, as Pashur and Jehucal are both mentioned in <reference osisRef="Jer.38.1">Jr 38:1</reference>, 2, as hearing Jeremiah's reply, which is identical with that in <reference osisRef="Jer.21.9">Jr 21:9</reference>, it is probable the two messages followed one another at a short interval; that in this <reference osisRef="Jer.37.3">Jr 37:3</reference>, and the answer, <reference osisRef="Jer.37.7-Jer.37.10">Jr 37:7-10</reference>, being the earlier of the two.<div eID="gen18572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18573" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zephaniah--</hi>an abettor of rebellion against God (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.25">Jr 29:25</reference>), though less virulent than many (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.29">Jr 29:29</reference>), punished accordingly (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.24-Jer.52.27">Jr 52:24-27</reference>). <div eID="gen18573" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10413"/><div sID="gen18575" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10413"/>5. After this temporary diversion, caused by Pharaoh in favor of Jerusalem, the Egyptians returned no more to its help (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.7">2Ki 24:7</reference>). Judea had the misfortune to lie between the two great contending powers, Babylon and Egypt, and so was exposed to the alternate inroads of the one or the other. Josiah, taking side with Assyria, fell in battle with Pharaoh-necho at Megiddo (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.29">2Ki 23:29</reference>). Zedekiah, seeking the Egyptian alliance in violation of his oath, was now about to be taken by Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.13">2Ch 36:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.15">Eze 17:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.17">17</reference>). <div eID="gen18575" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10419"/><div sID="gen18581" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10419"/><hi type="bold">12. Benjamin--</hi>to his own town, Anathoth.<div eID="gen18581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18582" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to separate himself--</hi>Margin translates, "to slip away," from a Hebrew root, "to be smooth," so, to slip away as a slippery thing that cannot be held. But it is not likely the prophet of God would flee in a dishonorable way; and "in the midst of the people" rather implies open departure along with others, than clandestine slipping away by mixing with the crowd of departing people. Rather, it means, to separate himself, or to divide his place of residence, so as to live partly here, partly there, without fixed habitation, going to and fro among the people [Ludovicus De Dieu]. Maurer translates, "to take his portion thence," to realize the produce of his property in Anathoth [Henderson], or to take possession of the land which he bought from Hanameel [Maurer]. <div eID="gen18582" type="x-p"/>
